Tu-134 has a short twinjet layout with rear-mounted engines and a glazed nose, a combination not seen on the Yak-42 or Douglas DC-9 and MD-80 variants.
Tu-154: Tu-154 has three rear-mounted jet engines, with one engine on each side of the aft fuselage and one fed from the base of the fin.
Tu-154 has a tall T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted on top of the vertical fin.
Tu-154 has a relatively small circular center-engine intake at the fin root, unlike the broader S-duct inlets of the L-1011 and 727-200.
Tu-154 has two main landing-gear units, and each main gear bogie carries three wheels in a row.
Tu-154 has six-wheel main landing gear, unlike the two-wheel main gear commonly seen on the 727-200 and Boeing 717.
Tu-154 has a long, pointed tailcone extending behind the side engines.
Tu-154 has a more slender fuselage than the wider-bodied L-1011.
Tu-154 has strongly swept wings that look more sharply angled than those of the Yak-42 and Boeing 717.
Tu-154 has low-mounted wings attached close to the bottom of the fuselage.
Tu-154 has a sharply pointed nose that projects well ahead of the cockpit windows.
Tu-154 has angular Soviet-style cockpit glazing with a distinctly faceted look around the nose.
Tu-154 lacks the lower navigator glazing seen on some other Soviet airliners in side or front-quarter views.
Tu-154 has side-mounted rear engines that sit close against the fuselage rather than hanging far out on pylons.
Tu-154 has overwing emergency exits above the wing area on the fuselage sides.
Tu-154 has a full-size passenger door near the front left side of the fuselage.
Tu-154 has another full-size passenger door near the rear left side of the fuselage.
Tu-154 has a rear fuselage that narrows noticeably toward the tail beneath the T-tail.
Tu-154 has a single vertical fin rather than the twin-fin arrangement seen on no common trijet airliner.
Tu-154 has a narrow-body fuselage that appears slimmer than the L-1011 and longer-looking than the shorter Boeing 717.
Tu-154 has a cleaner, more pointed rear fuselage profile than the 727-200, whose tail intake area appears broader and less needle-like.
Yak-42: Yak-42 is a smaller trijet than the 727-200, Tu-154, and L-1011, with a visibly shorter fuselage.
Yak-42 has a slimmer narrow-body fuselage than the broader-looking L-1011 and MD-11.
Yak-42 has a noticeably smaller wing than the larger-winged 727-200, Tu-154, L-1011, and MD-11.
Yak-42 has three rear-mounted engines with no engines under the wings.
Yak-42 has two side engines mounted tight against the rear fuselage.
Yak-42 has a third engine fed by a straight dorsal intake at the base of the fin.
Yak-42 has a straight fin-root intake for the center engine rather than the S-duct inlet seen on the 727-200 and Tu-154.
Yak-42 has circular engine intakes on all three tail-mounted nacelles.
Yak-42 has a T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted on top of the vertical fin.
Yak-42 has a relatively short, rounded nose compared with the longer, sharper noses of the Tu-154 and MD-11.
Yak-42 has compact cockpit glazing with a short flight-deck area.
Yak-42 has low-mounted swept wings attached below the cabin window line.
Yak-42 has bulky fuselage-side fairings or sponsons for the main landing gear.
Yak-42 shows prominent main-gear bulges along the lower fuselage sides, unlike the cleaner lower fuselage of many other trijets.
Yak-42 has a smooth wing underside without the large wing-root engine structure seen on underwing-jet airliners.
Yak-42 has a single vertical tail fin above the rear engine cluster.
Yak-42 has a rear fuselage that narrows into a compact tail-mounted engine group.
Yak-42 has a shorter overall cabin window row than the longer 727-200, Tu-154, L-1011, and MD-11.
Yak-42 has side-mounted rear engines that sit ahead of the tailplane, not on the wing roots.
Yak-42 has an overall compact Soviet trijet appearance with a short fuselage, small wing, and tall T-tail.
737-600: 737-600 is the shortest 737 Next Generation variant, with a visibly shorter fuselage than the 737-700.
737-600 has a noticeably shorter fuselage than the 737-800 and 737-900 members of the 737NG family.
737-600 is longer than the older 737-500, but still appears compact among Boeing narrow-body jets.
737-600 has the Boeing 737 nose shape, which is less rounded than the Airbus A318 or A319 nose.
737-600 has Boeing-style cockpit windows with angular, sharply segmented panes unlike the smoother Airbus A318 or A319 windshield layout.
737-600 has a taller vertical tail than the 737-500, matching the 737 Next Generation tail proportions.
737-600 has the revised 737NG wing shape, differing from the older wing planform seen on the 737-500.
737-600 often has blended winglets rising in a curved shape from the wingtips.
737-600 may also appear without winglets, showing plain pointed wingtips.
737-600 has two underwing turbofan nacelles that are generally larger than those on the 737-500.
737-600 has the flattened-bottom 737 engine nacelle shape rather than a perfectly round lower intake profile.
737-600 has one overwing emergency exit above each wing, a layout typical of the short 737NG fuselage.
737-600 has a short cabin with only a small number of passenger windows behind the wing compared with the longer 737-700.
737-600 has a short distance between the front passenger door and the wing, reflecting its compact fuselage.
737-600 has a short distance between the rear passenger door and the tail compared with the longer 737-700.
737-600 has low-mounted horizontal stabilizers on the rear fuselage, below the top of the fin.
737-600 has a conventional narrow-body stance with the main landing gear close under the fuselage.
737-600 has wings mounted low on the fuselage with one engine centered beneath each wing.
737-600 has a single vertical tail fin with a swept trailing edge typical of the 737NG family.
737-600 has a compact overall silhouette that is shorter than the Airbus A319 when viewed side-on.
747-300: 747-300 has a stretched upper-deck hump that extends noticeably farther aft than on the 747-100 and 747-200.
747-300 has a long row of upper-deck windows that runs farther back than on the 747-100 and 747-200.
747-300 has no winglets at the wingtips, unlike the 747-400.
747-300 has plain wingtip ends without the small upright winglets seen on the 747-400.
747-300 has an upper deck that is extended while the main fuselage length remains about the same as a 747-200.
747-300 has a side profile where the extra length is concentrated in the upper hump rather than in a longer lower fuselage.
747-300 has a clearly longer upper-deck cabin section behind the cockpit than the 747-100 or 747-200.
747-300 has an upper hump that reaches to around the wing-root area instead of ending much earlier like on the 747-100 and 747-200.
747-300 has fewer upper-deck windows than a full-length double-deck airliner such as the A380.
747-300 has a partial upper deck that stops well before the tail rather than continuing the full fuselage length.
747-300 has four underwing engines with the distinctive long upper-deck hump of the stretched-upper-deck 747 family member.
747-300 has the classic 747 nose shape under a long upper deck, not the shorter hump seen on the 747-100 or 747-200.
747-300 has upper-deck doors and windows confined to the forward half of the aircraft, but extending farther aft than on the 747-100 and 747-200.
747-300 has a long smooth upper-deck roofline that continues aft well beyond the short upper deck of earlier 747 variants.
747-300 has a wing profile similar to the 747-200 but without the wingtip winglets added on the 747-400.
747-300 has a main deck and tail layout like earlier 747s, with the most obvious change being the longer upper-deck hump.
747-300 has a stretched hump that makes the forward upper fuselage look longer than a 747-200 even though the lower fuselage is not obviously longer.
747-300 has a side silhouette closer to a 747-200 than a 747-400 except for the longer upper deck and lack of winglets.
747-300 has upper-deck window spacing over a longer section than the 747-100 and 747-200, creating a visibly extended hump.
747-300 has a forward fuselage where the upper deck ends far behind the cockpit but still far ahead of the tail.
757-300: 757-300 has a much longer fuselage than the 757-200, making it the clearly stretched member of the 757 family.
757-300 has an extremely long narrow-body fuselage that appears longer than a 737-800 or 737-900.
757-300 has noticeably long fuselage sections both ahead of and behind the wing compared with the 757-200.
757-300 has four full-size passenger doors visible on each side of the fuselage.
757-300 usually lacks the small overwing emergency exits commonly seen on many 757-200 and 737 variants.
757-300 has a longer uninterrupted cabin window line between doors than the 757-200.
757-300 has a long, slender fuselage-to-wing proportion that looks more stretched than on the 737-900.
757-300 has a taller ground stance than 737-family aircraft, with the fuselage sitting visibly higher above the runway.
757-300 has relatively tall main landing gear that gives the aircraft a higher-slung look than a 737-800 or 737-900.
757-300 has a long nose section ahead of the cockpit that appears more extended than on 737-family aircraft.
757-300 has 757-style cockpit and nose proportions, with a longer forward fuselage than a 737-800 or 737-900.
757-300 has a long, slim wing planform that looks more slender than the wing on a 737-800.
757-300 has a very long rear fuselage behind the wing, longer in appearance than on the 757-200.
757-300 has a narrow single-aisle fuselage, unlike the wider twin-aisle body of the 767-300.
757-300 has only one row of cabin windows across the fuselage width, unlike the wider-looking 767-300 body.
757-300 has underwing engines that appear smaller relative to its long fuselage than on a 737-800.
757-300 has a fuselage that looks exceptionally stretched for a twin-engine narrow-body jet.
757-300 has wider spacing between its forward and rear main doors than the shorter 757-200.
757-300 has a long center fuselage section around the wing that contributes to its distinctly elongated profile.
757-300 has an overall profile that combines a very long narrow fuselage, long nose, and high stance unlike the lower, shorter-looking 737-800 or 737-900.
ATR-42: ATR-42 has a noticeably shorter fuselage than the ATR-72, giving it a more compact overall body.
ATR-42 shows fewer passenger windows along the cabin side than the longer ATR-72.
ATR-42 has a short cabin length that makes the wing and engines look proportionally large relative to the fuselage.
ATR-42 has a high wing combined with prominent main-gear fairings mounted on the lower fuselage sides.
ATR-42 keeps its main landing gear in fuselage-side sponsons rather than in wing pods or nacelles.
ATR-42 has a rounded vertical tail tip and softly curved tail surfaces unlike the more angular Dash 8 family.
ATR-42 has a vertical fin with a smooth curved leading edge and a rounded top profile.
ATR-42 has low-mounted horizontal stabilizers with rounded tips that match the curved ATR tail style.
ATR-42 has a blunt, rounded nose that is less pointed than on the Saab 340.
ATR-42 has engine nacelles that appear chunky and deep under the high wing on its short fuselage.
ATR-42 has propeller discs that sit close to the forward half of the fuselage because the body is short.
ATR-42 has a shorter rear fuselage behind the wing than the ATR-72.
ATR-42 has a compact gap between the cockpit and the wing leading edge compared with the longer ATR-72.
ATR-42 has a shorter window row ahead of the wing than the ATR-72.
ATR-42 has a shorter window row behind the wing than the ATR-72.
ATR-42 has a fuselage-side gear fairing that forms a noticeable bulge below the cabin near the wing root.
ATR-42 has a taller-looking body-on-gear stance than the Saab 340 because of its high wing and fuselage-side gear fairings.
ATR-42 has a more rounded tail and rear-body shape than the boxier-looking DHC-8-100 and DHC-8-300.
ATR-42 has a shorter overall body than the DHC-8-300, making the aircraft look more compact from nose to tail.
ATR-42 has a slightly longer and fuller fuselage than the Saab 340 while keeping the same twin-turboprop high-wing layout.
